[Slides](09-ai-code-slides.html) · [Source](https://github.com/ArielOrtizBobea/aem6850/blob/main/fall-2026/sessions/09-ai-code.qmd)

How to work with a coding agent in your terminal as a fast research
assistant that needs clear instructions and close supervision. The first
part says what it has in front of it that a chat window does not, and
what you decide before it writes a line. The second part builds a small
project from an empty folder: a scraper for the Dyson School's Ph.D.
placements page, a postdoc flag, a country column, and the moment the
tool fills a column from memory. The third part writes the project's
`CLAUDE.md` and a read-only reviewer agent. Every step runs in RStudio's
Terminal tab.

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

::: {#before-class .callout-important title="Before class: install Claude Code, log in, and install rvest"}

About fifteen minutes, once, on the laptop you bring. Claude Code is not
on the free plan; it needs a paid Claude plan. Do all five steps; step 5
is the test.

**1. Subscribe to Claude Pro.** You will get a lot out of it this
semester; it is worth the investment. Cornell is working on access for
students; until that exists, plan on Pro: choose it on the [pricing
page](https://claude.com/pricing). If you decide not to subscribe,
follow the captured run on the slides in class and pair with a
neighbour for the two exercises.

**2. Install Claude Code.** *Mac:* in RStudio, **Tools → Terminal → New
Terminal**, paste this line, Enter:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
```

*Windows:* use PowerShell, not RStudio (Start, type `PowerShell`, open
it), paste this line, Enter:

```powershell
irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex
```

When it finishes, **quit and reopen RStudio**: the terminal you
installed from does not see the new program.

**3. Check the install.** **Tools → Terminal → New Terminal**, type
`claude --version`, Enter. It prints a version number followed by
`(Claude Code)`. `command not found`: quit and reopen RStudio. Windows,
still not found: add `%USERPROFILE%\.local\bin` to your user PATH, then
quit and reopen RStudio. Windows, and `claude` opens the Claude desktop
app instead: update the desktop app, then retry.

**4. Install rvest.** In RStudio's **Console** (not the Terminal), Enter
after each line:

```r
install.packages("rvest")
library(rvest)
```

The second line prints nothing when the install worked.

**5. Make the folder and log in (the test).** **File → New Project → New
Directory → New Project.** Directory name `placements`; *Create project
as subdirectory of* a folder you choose (`~/github` if you have one; on
Windows type `C:/Users/<your Windows username>/github` rather than
clicking Browse, which opens a folder OneDrive often syncs); do **not**
tick *Create a git repository*; **Create Project**. Then **Tools →
Terminal → New Terminal**; the prompt ends in `placements`. Type
`claude`, Enter. The first run asks a few set-up questions; take the
default text style. When it asks how to log in, choose the subscription
login. Your browser opens a Claude sign-in page: sign in with the
account from step 1 and follow the prompts back to the Terminal. When
it asks whether you trust this folder, **No, exit** is highlighted:
press the down arrow once to *Yes, I trust this folder*, Enter. A
welcome screen names the version, the model and your plan, and a folder
ending in `placements`. Type `/exit`, Enter. That is a pass. Anything
else: the "Things that bite" table at the end of this page lists the
fixes; still stuck, bring the laptop to class ten minutes early. Leave
the folder as it is; class starts from it.

:::

## Objectives {#objectives .smaller}

By the end of this session you can:

- Explain what Claude Code has in front of it that a chat window does
  not: every file in the folder, a terminal, git, and a file of standing
  instructions, `CLAUDE.md`.
- Start Claude Code in manual mode in an empty RStudio project and have
  it initialize the git repository.
- Hand the tool one task at a time, with a number you counted yourself
  on the web page it reads; let it run the script; compare.
- Read the box that shows each edit, and `git diff`, before accepting
  it, and find a value the tool typed from memory rather than read from
  the page.
- Write a `CLAUDE.md` for the project and a read-only reviewer agent,
  and say what each one changes.

Five things, and you do each of them on your own laptop in the two

## Chat, Cowork, Claude Code: one model, three harnesses {#harnesses}

| | Chat | Cowork | Claude Code |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Where it runs | a web page | the desktop app | your terminal, in one folder |
| How context arrives | you paste or attach it | from the folder you connect | from the folder, plus a file of standing instructions |
| Reads your files | no | every file in the folder | every file in the repository |
| Edits your files | no; you paste its output | yes, directly | yes; each edit shown as a diff first |
| Runs commands | on Anthropic's servers, on an attached file | on Anthropic's servers | on your laptop: R, git, anything in the terminal |
| Runs your R script | no; you run it | no; you run it | it can, when the prompt says so |
| What you read afterwards | the script you pasted | `git status`, `git diff` | the box that shows each edit, then `git diff` |

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
Same model in all three. The app around it, the harness, decides what
it can see and do. The last column is the only one that acts on your
laptop, which is why it asks first and why git is the safety net.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

Claude Code is the same Claude model as the chat window and Cowork, in
a third harness: a program in your terminal that runs in one folder.
The harness decides what the model can see and do. In a chat you paste
context in and copy text out. Cowork reads and writes the files in a
folder you connect and runs code in a sandbox on Anthropic's servers,
not on your laptop. Claude Code reads every file in the repository,
edits files after showing each edit as a diff, and runs commands in
your terminal: R, git, anything you could type there. That row is the
difference that matters. The other two never touch your machine; this
one does, which is why it asks before acting and why git is the safety
net.

Two other kinds of tool are not this page's subject. An inline tool
such as [GitHub Copilot in
RStudio](https://docs.posit.co/ide/user/ide/guide/tools/copilot.html)
proposes the next few lines in the editor and sees only the open file.
Terminal agents from other vendors work like Claude Code; the habits
on this page transfer to them.

:::

## How Claude Code works: the loop inside the tool {#tool-loop}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

![](figures/09-ai-code/D2-agent-loop.svg){fig-align="center" height="195" fig-alt="Five boxes left to right: 1 Prompt, your text plus CLAUDE.md; 2 Read, files, folders, command output; 3 Act, edit a file, run a command; 4 Check, read the result, decide the next step; 5 Reply, when nothing is left to do. A dashed red arrow from box 4 back to box 2 reads: again, until the task is done; in manual mode, step 3 asks you first."}

- It picks a tool: read, search, run a command, edit a file. The result
  comes back to it. Again, until done.
- Manual mode, today's setting: an edit, or a command that changes
  something, asks you first. Reading never asks.
- A session starts empty. What carries over is on disk: files, commits,
  `CLAUDE.md`.

::: {.notes}
The model writes text only. Every read, run and edit is a request the
harness carries out and reports back. In manual mode the requests that
change something come to you as approval boxes.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

![The loop inside the tool. In manual mode, step 3 stops and asks you before an edit or a command that changes something.](figures/09-ai-code/D2-agent-loop.svg){fig-align="center" fig-alt="Five boxes left to right: 1 Prompt, your text plus CLAUDE.md; 2 Read, files, folders, command output; 3 Act, edit a file, run a command; 4 Check, read the result, decide the next step; 5 Reply, when nothing is left to do. A dashed red arrow from box 4 back to box 2 reads: again, until the task is done; in manual mode, step 3 asks you first."}

Inside the tool runs a loop. Your prompt goes to the model together
with a hidden system prompt and, if the folder has one, `CLAUDE.md`.
The model writes text and nothing else; it cannot open a file or run a
command itself. So it writes a request for a tool, and the harness
carries it out: read a file, search the folder, run a command in the
terminal, edit a file. The tool's result comes back to the model as
text, and the model decides the next step. That repeats until nothing
is left to do; then you get a reply. Anthropic's page [How Claude Code
works](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/how-claude-code-works) describes
the same loop in three phases: gather context, take action, verify
results. In today's project the tool runs the script and fixes it when
it fails; the third phase is still yours, because only you know the
number the script must reproduce.

In manual mode the loop stops at every edit and at every command that
changes something and asks you; reading is free. You can stop it too:
Esc interrupts. Everything the model has in front of it at a given
moment is its context: the system prompt, `CLAUDE.md`, your prompts,
every file it read and every command output so far. A new session
starts with an empty context. What carries over is what is on disk:
the files, the commits, and `CLAUDE.md`.

:::

## What changes when a tool can edit your files {#what-changes}

- It can read any file in the repository. Nothing private goes in that folder.
- Its edits land on disk, not in a chat.
- It can run commands, including git.
- It shows every edit as a diff before it lands. You accept or refuse.
- Anything it reads goes to Anthropic's servers. Restricted data stays
  out; develop on a public or synthetic sample.
- What is right is still your call.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
Each of these needs a habit; git and reading the diff are the two.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

Four things change. It can read any file in the repository, so what it
sees is not what you pasted but what is on disk. Its edits land on disk,
not in a chat window. It can run commands, including scripts and git.
Every edit appears as a diff before it lands; that diff is the one thing
you must read. Anything it reads is sent to Anthropic's servers for
processing, so check your data use agreements before pointing it at
confidential files; the practical workaround is to let it develop the
code on a synthetic or public sample with the same structure, and to
run the final code yourself on the restricted data. The verification is
yours; the tool has no way to compare the number it produced with the
number you meant.

:::

## You decide the question; it writes the code {#you-decide}

- It is strong at writing, refactoring and debugging code. It is weak
  at judging whether a specification answers your question.
- Decide the estimand, the sample, the weights, the fixed effects and
  the clustering yourself. Then ask it to implement them.
- Let it choose and it picks something plausible. Plausible is not the
  same as right.
- A fact it did not read is a guess: a function's arguments, a
  citation, a fact about the world. Check the documentation, the paper,
  the source.
- You must be able to explain every line. Ask it to explain rather
  than write, and it becomes a tutor.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
Treat it as a fast, capable research assistant that needs clear
instructions and close supervision. The third bullet is today's
project: a country column.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

Claude Code is most useful when you treat it as a fast, capable
research assistant that needs clear instructions and close
supervision. It is strong at writing, refactoring and debugging code.
It is weaker at judging whether a specification answers your question.
So you own the identification and it owns the plumbing: decide the
estimand, the fixed effects, the clustering and the sample restrictions
yourself, then ask it to implement them. If you let it choose, it will
pick something plausible, and plausible is not the same as right.

The same rule covers facts. It can misremember a function's arguments,
especially in less common packages; it can cite papers that do not
exist or misstate what they found; it can fill a column with countries
it never read anywhere. Check documentation and citations yourself, and
treat any value it did not read from your data or your page as a guess
until you have checked it. Today's project shows this with a country
column.

For students, understanding comes first. It is possible to produce
working code without understanding it. The rule in this course is that
you can explain every line of code in your analysis. Ask the tool to
explain its code rather than only write it; that turns it into a tutor.
A line you still cannot explain after the explanation is a line to
replace with one you can.

:::

## The main risk is silent errors, not crashes {#silent-errors}

- Code that fails is easy to fix. Code that runs and is wrong is the
  danger.
- The usual shapes: a merge that drops or duplicates rows; `NA`s
  handled silently; a unit mismatch; an estimation call that differs a
  little from what you asked.
- Three defenses: explicit checks, `stopifnot()` on row counts, unique
  keys and value ranges; estimators tried on simulated data with known
  parameters; the merge and the regression call read by you.
- Git is the safety net: commit before each task, read the diff after
  it, `git restore` puts a file back.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
Every defense is something you do. The tool can write the check; it
cannot decide what the right row count is.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

Code that fails is easy to fix: the error names the line. Code that
runs but is wrong is the real danger, and it is the common case with a
tool that writes plausible code quickly. The usual shapes are a merge
that drops or duplicates rows, `NA`s handled in a way you did not
expect, a unit mismatch, and an estimation call that differs slightly
from what you asked for: a different standard error, a sample
restriction applied one step too late.

Three defenses, all yours. Ask for explicit checks, `stopifnot()` on
row counts after a merge, on unique keys, on value ranges; the tool
writes them well once you name the number. Test estimators on
simulated data with known parameters before running them on real data;
if the estimate does not recover the parameter you planted, the code is
wrong, whatever the transcript says. And read the key lines yourself,
the merges and the regression call above all.

Git is the safety net around all of it. Commit before each task, so the
diff afterwards is exactly what the tool did. Review that diff. Claude
Code edits many files quickly, and git is what lets you see what
changed and roll back with `git restore`. If you do not use git yet,
this tool is the best reason to start.

:::

## Small tasks, short sessions, a plan before code {#small-tasks}

- One well-defined task per session: "build the county-year panel",
  "write the event-study plot". "Do the analysis" produces large vague
  code.
- Performance drops as the context fills with old material. Start a
  fresh conversation between unrelated tasks (the `/clear` command).
- Anything with a merge or a panel build: "Describe your approach
  before writing any code." Read the plan; fix misunderstandings there,
  where they are cheap.
- Conventions you would otherwise repeat go once into `CLAUDE.md`, a
  file it reads at every launch: base R only, never touch `data/raw/`,
  relative paths, a clean session, a master script, seeds,
  `sessionInfo()` saved with results.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
Plan mode exists for the third bullet; the sentence works in any mode.
CLAUDE.md is the sixth part of today.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

Keep tasks small and sessions short. Everything the model has in front
of it competes for its attention, and performance drops as the context
fills with old material. Give one well-defined task per session, such
as "build the county-year panel" or "write the event-study plot", and
use `/clear` between unrelated tasks. Large vague requests like "do the
analysis" produce large vague code that nobody can check.

Plan before it writes code. For anything nontrivial, use plan mode
(Shift+Tab cycles to it) or simply write "Describe your approach before
writing any code." Read the plan. Fix misunderstandings at that stage,
when they are cheap. This habit matters most for data construction
steps like merges and panel building, and today's project shows what
it would have caught.

Build reproducibility in from the start, as standing rules rather than
reminders: a master script that runs the whole pipeline in order,
package versions locked (`renv` is one way), a seed for anything
stochastic, `sessionInfo()` saved with the results. The tool follows
such rules reliably once they are written in `CLAUDE.md`, the file it
reads at the start of every session; the sixth part of this page writes
one for the project.

:::

## Two rules: a clean git state, and the diff over the transcript {#two-rules}

- **Start from a clean git state.** `git status` clean before the
  prompt; afterwards the diff is exactly what the model did.
- **Trust the diff, not the transcript.** What it did, not what its
  replies say it did.
- Commit before each task; read every diff before you commit;
  `git restore` puts a file back.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
Rule one is why rule two works. A dirty tree mixes your edits with its
edits, and the diff no longer shows what the model did. The diff-reading
habit from the git session is the whole reason rule two is usable.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

Rule one: start from a clean git state. `git status` prints `nothing to
commit, working tree clean` before you type a prompt; then every line
the diff shows afterwards is the model's, and none is yours. Rule two:
trust the diff, not the transcript. The transcript says what the tool
claims it did. The diff shows what it did. When they disagree, the diff
wins.

:::

## The project: the Ph.D. placements page, from an empty folder {#project}

- The page: [Recent job placements, Ph.D. in Applied Economics & Management](https://business.cornell.edu/admissions/graduate/phd-aem/for-hire/).
  One table: year, name, position, organization. 109 rows when captured.
- Four prompts, one task each: start git; read the table into a CSV
  (scraping); flag the postdocs; add each organization's country. Then:
  where the countries came from.
- The prompts tell the tool to run the script and fix it when it fails.
  You check every number against the page.
- The folder: `placements`, no git yet. Once, in the Console:
  `install.packages("rvest")`, the R package that reads web pages.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
A public page, one table, and a column the page does not have. The
instructor's terminal is on the projector; the slides carry the prompts
and what came back.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

The project is small and real. The Dyson School lists its recent Ph.D.
placements on one public page as a table with four columns: year, name,
position, organization. We scrape it into a CSV, add a column that
flags postdocs, and add a column with the country of each organization.
The page does not state the country, and that is the point of the
third prompt.

Two things differ from a chat. The prompts tell the tool to run the
script and fix it when it fails, so the tool is the loop; your job is
the check, a number you count on the page before you believe the
number on the screen. And everything starts from an empty folder: no
repository, no script, nothing the tool did not write in front of you.

Every prompt on this page is the exact text of one captured run on
2026-09-21, and every number is from that run: 109 rows, 16 of them in
2026, 25 postdocs. The page grows every year, so the numbers on your
screen will differ. The prompts, the checks and the lesson do not.

:::

## The steps, from an empty folder to the first prompt {#steps .smaller}

1. RStudio: **File → New Project → New Directory → New Project**. Name
   `placements`, inside `~/github`. Do not tick *Create a git
   repository*. **Create Project**.
2. Console, once: `install.packages("rvest")`.
3. **Tools → Terminal → New Terminal.** The prompt ends in `placements`.
4. Type `claude --permission-mode manual`, Enter.
5. The trust question: ↓ once to *Yes, I trust this folder*, Enter.
6. The welcome screen: the folder ends in `placements`; the status line
   reads `⏸ manual mode on`.
7. Paste Prompt 0. Read each box, `1. Yes`.
8. **Tools → Terminal → New Terminal** again (Terminal 2): `git log --oneline`.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
Eight steps, one slide each from here to Prompt 0. Nobody types ahead:
we do them together, and the exercises repeat them.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

The whole path, in order; the next six sections take the steps one at a
time. The RStudio project is the folder: *New Project* creates
`~/github/placements` with one file in it, `placements.Rproj`, and every
Terminal you open from Tools → Terminal starts there, so there is
nothing to navigate. Leave the git box unticked: Prompt 0 asks the tool
to do that part, and you watch it happen. If you did Before class, steps
1 and 2 are done; open the project (File → Recent Projects →
`placements`) and start at step 3.

Without RStudio, the same eight steps in a terminal:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/github/placements
cd ~/github/placements
claude --permission-mode manual
```

then the trust question, the welcome screen, and Prompt 0; git goes in a
second terminal window opened in the same folder.

:::

3. **Console**: where you run the script
4. **Files pane**: what it wrote

::: {.notes}
It runs in the Terminal tab, inside the project, so the paths are the

![One RStudio window: Claude Code in the Terminal tab, the Console free for running scripts, the Files pane showing what was written. Claude Code runs in RStudio's Terminal tab, the tab where git commands
go, opened inside the project so the folder it sees is the repository.
The Console stays free, so the script it writes runs where scripts
always run: Session → Restart R, then Source. The Files pane shows what
it wrote. Enlarge the Terminal pane before a prompt: drag the divider
up, or use the maximize icon in the pane's corner. An approval box for a
twenty-line file does not fit the default pane.

:::

## Launching Claude Code in manual mode {#launch}

```bash
claude --permission-mode manual
```

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

- Manual mode: it asks before every edit and every command that changes something.
- The status line must read `⏸ manual mode on`.
- Any other mode: `/exit`, then this line again.

::: {.notes}
Use this line, not bare `claude`, until reading diffs is a habit.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

One line in the Terminal tab launches it in manual mode, where it reads
freely but asks before every edit and every command that changes
something. Depending on the plan, a session may otherwise start in
auto mode, where a second model reviews actions instead of you. The
status line above the prompt says which mode you are in; it must read
`⏸ manual mode on` for everything today. Shift+Tab cycles the modes; if
the keystroke does not reach the tool inside RStudio's terminal, quit
with `/exit` and relaunch with the line above. The mode's configuration
name is `default`, so `--permission-mode default` launches the same
mode.

:::

## Reading the welcome screen {#welcome}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

:::: {.columns}

1. **Version**: the number varies; any current one
2. **Model · plan**: the model in use and your plan; wording varies
3. **Folder**: ends in `placements`
4. **`❯`**: type here, Enter sends
5. **Status line**: `⏸ manual mode on`

The captured account is not a student account; on your laptop the second line names your plan and its model, in wording that varies.](figures/09-ai-code/S02-welcome.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="The Claude Code welcome screen: Claude Code v2.1.258, the model and plan line, the folder ~/github/gapminder-practice, the prompt box, and the status line reading manual mode on."}

Four lines matter: the version; the model and plan (yours differ from
the captured account's); the folder; and
the status line, `⏸ manual mode on`. The folder must end in
`placements` (on Windows it starts with `C:/Users/`); the captured
screen shows another folder. The `❯` is
where a prompt goes; Enter sends it.

Every Claude Code screen on this page comes from real runs, captured in
September 2026 with the version the welcome screen shows; the RStudio
screens are separate captures. The interface changes between versions,
and replies vary from run to run: the wording of a summary, sometimes
the code. The steps do not.

:::

## Keys, commands, and a second Terminal tab {#keys}

| Key or command | Does |
|:--|:--|
| Enter | sends the prompt |
| Esc | interrupts; on a question, declines |
| ↑ | brings back the previous prompt |
| `/clear` | new conversation, same folder |
| `/exit` (or Ctrl+C twice) | leaves Claude Code |
| Tools → Terminal → New Terminal | a second tab for git |

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
Esc interrupts whatever it is doing. Open a second Terminal tab for git,
so you can read what it did without leaving the tool.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

Five keys a novice needs, and one RStudio habit: Claude Code occupies
its Terminal tab, so git commands go in a second one.
Tools → Terminal → New Terminal opens *Terminal 2*; the dropdown at the
top of the Terminal pane switches between them. Leave Claude Code in
Terminal 1 and type git in Terminal 2. If the Terminal shows R's `>`
prompt instead of `❯`, you typed `claude` in the Console: Tools →
Terminal → New Terminal, then again.

![Two Terminal tabs: Claude Code stays in Terminal 1, git goes in Terminal 2. The dropdown switches between them.](figures/09-ai-code/S13-terminal-dropdown.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="RStudio's Terminal pane with its dropdown open, listing Terminal 1 running Claude Code and Terminal 2 at the shell prompt, both circled in red."}

:::

`git init`, a `.gitignore`, a first commit. In the captured run it
listed the folder, wrote `.gitignore` (a *Create file* box, three

... && git log --oneline && git status`, shown in full in a *Bash

line in the message naming the model. That is a fair record of who
wrote what, and it belongs in your disclosure too.

## One task per prompt: the four parts {#prompt-shape}

- **The goal**: what the script must do, with names for its inputs and
  its output.
- **The mistake to avoid, named**: the plausible wrong reading. Call it
  the failure mode.
- **The file to write, and where**: `code/<name>.R`.
- **What not to do**: no other files, no git; and whether to run it.
- Prompt 0 had three of the four; the next prompt has all four. Paste
  them; do not retype them.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
Part two is the one novices leave out. Prompt 3, the country column,
is what happens without it.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

A prompt that hands the tool one task has four parts, in any order.
The goal: what the script must do, with names for what it reads and
what it writes. The mistake to avoid, named: the plausible wrong
reading a careful person could take; call it the failure mode. The file
to write and where: which file, in which folder. What not to do: no
other files, no git, and whether to run it or leave the run to you.
The fourth part is what keeps the diff small enough to read. Prompt 0
had a goal, a file and a "what not to do"; the next prompt, the
scraper, has all four. Every prompt on this page is the exact text of
the captured run; paste it, do not retype it.

:::

## Scoping a delegation: one task, one file {#scoping}

| Too big to check | Right-sized |
|:--|:--|
| "Do my analysis of the placements." | "Write `code/placements.R`: the table at ... saved as `data/placements.csv`, four columns." |
| "Make a report on placements." | "Add a column `postdoc`: TRUE when the position is a postdoc. Change nothing else." |
| "Fix my script." | "Only the country column is wrong; replace the table in the code with a data file I fill in." |

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

- If you cannot count one case on the page, the delegation is too large.

::: {.notes}
One function, one file, one case you can do on paper. Bigger tasks are
this, several times.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

You cannot check "Do my analysis of the placements", because nothing
about it has a value you can count. "Add a column `postdoc`" can, with
the browser's find box. The unit of delegation is one task with one
output and one small case, in one file. A bigger task is several of
these in a row, each checked before the next, and one per session.

:::

## Three questions before you delegate {#three-tests}

1. Can you name the mistake to avoid?
2. Can you count one case by hand, on the page or in rows you can see?
3. Can you read the whole diff in five minutes?

- Any no: split the task.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
If any answer is no, split the task.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

Before pasting, three questions. Can you name the mistake to avoid? Can you
count one case by hand, on the page or in rows you can see? Can you read
the diff in five minutes? A no to any of them means the task is too large; split
it until all three are yes.

:::

## The five-step delegation loop {#five-steps}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

![](figures/09-ai-code/D1-five-step-loop.svg){fig-align="center" height="250" fig-alt="Five boxes left to right: 1 Explain, the goal and the failure mode; 2 Delegate, one task, one file; 3 Work it out, one small case by hand; 4 Verify, run, compare, read the diff; 5 Keep, the hand check as a line in the script. A dashed red arrow from box 4 back to box 2 reads: they disagree, ask for a patch, then verify again."}

- Next: the table read from the page. The count on paper: one year's
  rows, counted on the page.
- Then two columns, each with its own count.
- The permanent check: the counts written into the script, dated.

::: {.notes}
Step three is the one people skip. Without a value on paper, step four
is only watching a script run.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

![The five-step delegation loop. When the value on paper and the printed value disagree, the arrow goes back to step 2 as a patch request.](figures/09-ai-code/D1-five-step-loop.svg){fig-align="center" fig-alt="Five boxes left to right: 1 Explain, the goal and the failure mode; 2 Delegate, one task, one file; 3 Work it out, one small case by hand; 4 Verify, run, compare, read the diff; 5 Keep, the hand check as a line in the script. A dashed red arrow from box 4 back to box 2 reads: they disagree, ask for a patch, then verify again."}

Every delegation runs the same five steps. State the goal and the
mistake you do not want (the failure mode). Delegate one task. Count by
hand what it must return on a case small enough to check, on the page
or from rows you can see, before anything runs. Run it and compare the printed
value with the one on paper; if they disagree, read the diff, ask for a
patch, run again. Then write the hand check into the script as a line
that stops it when the value drifts (`stopifnot()`), so the next run
checks itself. The value on paper comes from the data, not from a
guess; that is what makes step 4 a comparison and not an impression.

This loop wraps the loop inside the tool. The tool gathers context,
acts and checks its own result; you decide what right means and check
it once more from outside. Anthropic's
[best practices for Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices)
give the same advice in their own words: state verification criteria
in the prompt (an example input and its expected output), scope the
task to one file and one scenario, describe the symptom and what fixed
looks like when asking for a fix, and, in the list of common failures,
"If you can't verify it, don't ship it." The five steps are that advice
arranged for a novice who runs the script and reads the diff in
person.

:::

## Prompt 1: the scraper, run until it works {#prompt-scrape}

```{.markdown filename="Prompt to paste into Claude Code (captured run)"}
Write code/placements.R. It reads the table "Recent job placements" at
https://business.cornell.edu/admissions/graduate/phd-aem/for-hire/ and saves
it as data/placements.csv with the page's four columns, year, name, position,
organization, one row per graduate. Use the rvest package for the HTML and
base R for the rest. Run it with Rscript code/placements.R; if it fails, fix
the script and run again. Then show me the first five rows and the number of
rows. Do not use git.
```

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

- Two *Bash command* boxes before any file: it looked at the page's two
  tables first. Then *Create file*, then `Rscript`.
- What came back: "Wrote 109 rows"; the first five rows; how it chose
  the table.
- The hand check, on the page: count the 2026 rows. 16. Console:
  `sum(read.csv("data/placements.csv")$year == 2026)`.

::: {.notes}
Goal, artifact and path, what not to do, and this time: run it. The
check is one year's rows, small enough to count on the page.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

The prompt has the four parts: the goal with names, the artifact and
its path, what not to do, and one more sentence than before: run it,
and fix it if it fails. In the captured run the tool first ran two
short R commands to look at the page (the page has two tables, one for
alumni for hire and one for placements), then wrote the script, ran it,
and reported: 109 rows, the first five, and how it chose the table. It
ran cleanly the first time; a scraper often does not, and the sentence
"if it fails, fix the script and run again" is what lets the tool
iterate without you.

The check is yours. The total, 109, is too long to count by hand, so
count one year: the 2026 rows sit at the top of the table, sixteen of
them when captured. In the Console, `sum(read.csv("data/placements.csv")$year
== 2026)` must print the same number. If it does not, the scraper
dropped or duplicated rows, which is exactly the silent error a clean
run hides.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}

````{.default}
⏺ Write(<project>code/placements.R)
  # Scrape "Recent job placements" (Ph.D. in Applied Economics & Management)
  # from the Dyson "for hire" page and save it as data/placements.csv.
  # Uses rvest for the HTML and base R for everything else.
  
  library(rvest)
  
  url <- "https://business.cornell.edu/admissions/graduate/phd-aem/for-hire/"
  out <- file.path("data", "placements.csv")
  
  page   <- read_html(url)
  tables <- html_elements(page, "table")
  
  # The page has several tables (e.g. "Currently for hire"); pick the one whose
  # header is Year / Name / Position / Organization rather than relying on its
  # position or TablePress id.
  wanted  <- c("year", "name", "position", "organization")
  headers <- lapply(tables, function(tb) tolower(html_text2(html_elements(tb, "th"))))
  hit     <- which(vapply(headers, function(h) identical(h, wanted), logical(1)))
  if (length(hit) != 1) {
    stop("Expected exactly one placements table with columns ",
         paste(wanted, collapse = ", "), "; found ", length(hit))
  }
  
  placements <- as.data.frame(html_table(tables[[hit]], header = TRUE),
                              stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  names(placements) <- wanted
  placements$year   <- as.integer(placements$year)
  for (v in wanted[-1]) placements[[v]] <- trimws(placements[[v]])
  
  # Drop any completely empty rows (spacer rows in the table) but keep one
  # row per graduate otherwise.
  placements <- placements[placements$name != "", ]
  rownames(placements) <- NULL
  
  dir.create(dirname(out), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
  write.csv(placements, out, row.names = FALSE)
  
  cat("Wrote", nrow(placements), "rows to", out, "\n")
````

1. **Create file**, and the path

5. **`3. No` or Esc**: refuse

::: {.notes}

Yes, 2. Yes, and switch to accept edits, 3. No."}

In manual mode the tool shows the file before it exists. The box names
the action (*Create file*), the path, every line of the file, and a
question with three answers. `1. Yes` (Enter) writes the file. `2. Yes,
and switch to accept edits` turns the edit questions off for the
session; leave it today. `3. No`, or Esc, refuses and lets you say why.
For the scraper, the lines to read before pressing anything are the
ones that pick the table; the next section shows them.

## git diff \-\-staged on the scraper: the lines to read {#diff-new-file}

```bash
git add code/placements.R
git diff --staged
```

```r
wanted  <- c("year", "name", "position", "organization")
headers <- lapply(tables, function(tb) tolower(html_text2(html_elements(tb, "th"))))
hit     <- which(vapply(headers, function(h) identical(h, wanted), logical(1)))
if (length(hit) != 1) {
  stop("Expected exactly one placements table with columns ", ...)
}
```

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

- A new file: every line is a `+`. Read it top to bottom once.
- These lines matter: it picks the table by its header, not by its
  position, and stops if there is not exactly one.
- A line you cannot explain: ask for an explanation before you accept.
  `vapply()` and `identical()` are two to ask about.

::: {.notes}
The transcript said how it chose the table; the diff shows it. Now you
have read it rather than been told it.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

A new file has no earlier version, so `git diff` alone shows nothing;
`git add` it, then `git diff --staged` prints every line with a `+`.
That is the whole of what the tool did. Read it once from the top. The
lines above are the ones that carry the risk: they collect every table
on the page, keep the one whose header is exactly the four names, and
stop the script if there is not exactly one such table. A future change
to the page fails loudly instead of writing the wrong table.

Three functions a novice may not know, and may ask the tool to explain
or replace: `html_elements()` finds every element of a kind on the page;
`vapply()` applies a function to each table and promises a logical
result; `identical()` compares two vectors as a whole. "Explain
`vapply` on line 19, then rewrite it as a `for` loop if that is
clearer" is a fair prompt. The full file as written by prompt 1:

```{.r filename="code/placements.R (after prompt 1)"}
# Scrape "Recent job placements" (Ph.D. in Applied Economics & Management)
# from the Dyson "for hire" page and save it as data/placements.csv.
# Uses rvest for the HTML and base R for everything else.

library(rvest)

url <- "https://business.cornell.edu/admissions/graduate/phd-aem/for-hire/"
out <- file.path("data", "placements.csv")

page   <- read_html(url)
tables <- html_elements(page, "table")

# The page has several tables (e.g. "Currently for hire"); pick the one whose
# header is Year / Name / Position / Organization rather than relying on its
# position or TablePress id.
wanted  <- c("year", "name", "position", "organization")
headers <- lapply(tables, function(tb) tolower(html_text2(html_elements(tb, "th"))))
hit     <- which(vapply(headers, function(h) identical(h, wanted), logical(1)))
if (length(hit) != 1) {
  stop("Expected exactly one placements table with columns ",
       paste(wanted, collapse = ", "), "; found ", length(hit))
}

placements <- as.data.frame(html_table(tables[[hit]], header = TRUE),
                            stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
names(placements) <- wanted
placements$year   <- as.integer(placements$year)
for (v in wanted[-1]) placements[[v]] <- trimws(placements[[v]])

# Drop any completely empty rows (spacer rows in the table) but keep one
# row per graduate otherwise.
placements <- placements[placements$name != "", ]
rownames(placements) <- NULL



dir.create(dirname(out), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
write.csv(placements, out, row.names = FALSE)

cat("Wrote", nrow(placements), "rows to", out, "\n")
```

:::

## How to judge a model's diff: five questions {#judge-diff}

1. **Files**: only the ones you named? (`git status`)
2. **Removals**: every `-` line asked for? Read these first.
3. **The line that does the work**: does it do what you asked, and only that?
4. **Names and constants**: yours? A table of literals is a constant you did not supply.
5. **A line you cannot explain**: ask before you accept, or ask for one
   you can read.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
Five questions, in this order. The second one is where an unasked
change hides.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

Five questions, in order, every time, whether the diff is in the
approval box or in `git diff`. Are the only changed files the ones you
named (`git status`)? Are there `-` lines, and did you ask for each
removal? Which line does the math, and does it match the failure mode
you named? Are the names and constants yours (the argument names, no
bare numbers)? Is there a line you cannot explain? For the last one,
ask for an explanation before accepting, or ask for a version that uses
only functions you know. Removals first: a removal you did not ask for
is the dangerous kind. Question 4 is the one the country column fails:
sixteen country names and a default are constants, and you did not
supply them. Exercise 2 walks these five on that edit.

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

*Paired with a neighbour?* One laptop, two readers: the one not typing
reads each box aloud before `1. Yes`. A *Bash command* box that runs

position, organization` and stop unless exactly one matches.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

page grew. The picking lines: `wanted`, `headers`, `hit`, and the

:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
Debrief (2 min). Everyone's row count is the same number: the page is
one source. A laptop whose year count differs from its page count:
which rows are missing or doubled? That is the silent error, found.

When it fails, say:

- `command not found: claude`: Before class step 2; quit and reopen
  RStudio; pair up for now.
- The Terminal shows R's `>` prompt instead of `❯`: they typed `claude`
  in the Console. Tools → Terminal → New Terminal, then again.
- The status line says auto mode: `/exit`, then
  `claude --permission-mode manual`.
- The trust question again: the terminal is outside the project; Tools →
  Terminal → New Terminal from inside it.
- `there is no package called 'rvest'`: `install.packages("rvest")` in
  the Console; then tell the tool to run again.
- No Bash box for git and the reply says it cannot run commands: the
  status line is not manual, or the folder was not trusted; `/exit`,
  relaunch, look at the status line.
- The box never appears and it prints code instead: it wrote nothing;
  ask again with the artifact line, "Write code/placements.R", first.
- The row count differs from the page: the page changed since capture;
  the count for one year is the check that matters.
:::

## Prompt 2: a postdoc flag {#prompt-postdoc}

```{.markdown filename="Prompt to paste into Claude Code (captured run)"}
Add a column postdoc to the table before it is saved: TRUE when the position
is a postdoc, FALSE otherwise. Change nothing else. Run it again and tell me
how many rows are TRUE.
```

```diff
+# Flag postdoc positions; spellings on the page include "Postdoc", "Post-doc",
+# "Post Doctoral Fellow" and "Postdoctoral Associate".
+placements$postdoc <- grepl("post[- ]?doc", placements$position, ignore.case = TRUE)
```

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

- It looked at the spellings first: eleven of them. One pattern covers
  the three shapes: joined, hyphen, space.
- 25 of 109 rows are TRUE. One judgment call in its reply: a row listed
  as both a postdoc and an assistant professor.
- The hand check, Ctrl+F on the page: "postdoc" 15, "post-doc" 9,
  "post doc" 1. 25.

::: {.notes}
The edit box shows one comment and one line. A pattern you cannot read
is question 5: ask it to explain `[- ]?`.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

A one-line task with a check you can do in the browser. The tool first
printed every position containing "post", eleven spellings from
"Post-doc" to "Earth Institute Postdoctoral Fellow", then added one
comment and one line: a pattern that accepts "postdoc", "post-doc" and
"post doc" in any case. It ran the script again and reported 25 of 109
rows TRUE, and flagged one judgment call, a graduate listed as
"Postdoctoral Associate; Assistant Professor of Economics", counted as
TRUE.

The hand check is the browser's find box on the page. Find is not
case-sensitive, so "postdoc" counts every "Postdoc" and "Postdoctoral",
15 when captured; "post-doc" counts the hyphenated ones, 9; "post doc"
counts the one with a space. 25. A pattern that matched only "postdoc"
would have printed 15 and run clean; that is the failure mode this
check catches, and it is worth trying on purpose in the practice set.

:::

## The approval box for an edit: red and green lines {#approve-edit}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](figures/09-ai-code/S05-edit-dialog-diff.png){height="415" fig-alt="Claude Code's edit approval box: Update(code/lifeexp_by_continent.R), Edit file, a diff with line 1 removed in red and rewritten in green, line 5 removed in red and replaced by two green lines using sum, and the question Do you want to make this edit? with the answers 1. Yes, 2. Yes, and switch to accept edits, 3. No."}
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
1. **`-` red**: what goes. Read these first.
2. **`+` green**: what arrives
3. **Line 1**: changed unasked; harmless, but read it
4. **`1. Yes`** accepts; **Esc** refuses
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
The box is from another project; the shape is the same. Two red lines
where one was asked for: the extra one is a comment. Notice it, then
accept it. The country edit has no red lines and thirty green ones.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

![The approval box for an edit. Two red lines: the line asked about, and a header comment rewritten without being asked. The screen is from another project; the box is the same.](figures/09-ai-code/S05-edit-dialog-diff.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="Claude Code's edit approval box: Update(code/lifeexp_by_continent.R), Edit file, a diff with line 1 removed in red and rewritten in green, line 5 removed in red and replaced by two green lines using sum, and the question Do you want to make this edit? with the answers 1. Yes, 2. Yes, and switch to accept edits, 3. No."}

The tool shows an edit as a diff before it lands: removed lines in red
with `-`, added lines in green with `+`. Read every red line first. In
the box shown, two lines go: the line asked about, and a header
comment the tool rewrote although nobody asked. It is harmless, and it
is the kind of extra change the red lines exist to show. `1. Yes`
accepts. The postdoc edit is one comment and one line, all green; the
country edit is thirty green lines, and every country name in them is
question 4.

:::

## Writing the hand counts into the script {#hand-check}

```diff
 placements$postdoc <- grepl("post[- ]?doc", placements$position, ignore.case = TRUE)
+
+# Counted on the page on 2026-09-21: 16 rows for 2026; postdoc spellings
+# 15 + 9 + 1. When the page changes this stops the script: recount, then edit.
+stopifnot(sum(placements$year == 2026) == 16, sum(placements$postdoc) == 25)
```

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

- You type it, in RStudio. The checker is not the thing being checked.
- The numbers are the ones you counted; the comment says when.
- When the page changes, the script stops and says so. That is the
  point, not a nuisance.
- Then commit: `git add code/placements.R`, `git commit -m "Scrape
  placements, flag postdocs (Claude Code); two hand counts"`.

::: {.notes}
Step five of the loop. Two counts you did by hand, now run on every
Source. The commit message says who wrote what.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

The hand counts were done once, by a person. They become a line the
script runs every time. Type it yourself in RStudio, after the `postdoc`
line and before `write.csv`, save, Session → Restart R, Source: no
error. The checker is not the thing being checked, so in a graded
repository typing it yourself is the default.

The counts will go stale: the page adds a class every year. When it
does, the script stops with `Error: sum(placements$year == 2026) == 16
is not TRUE`, which is the script telling you that the source changed
and the counts need redoing. Recount on the page, edit the numbers and
the date in the comment, run again. A check that never fails is a
check on nothing.

Then commit, with a message that says who wrote what: the scraper and
the flag are the tool's, patched by nobody; the counts are yours. The
same sentence fills the disclosure block of a submission.

```bash
git add code/placements.R
git commit -m "Scrape placements, flag postdocs (Claude Code); two hand counts"
git log --oneline
#> <your hash> Scrape placements, flag postdocs (Claude Code); two hand counts
#> <your hash> New project
```

:::

## Prompt 3: a country column {#prompt-country}

```{.markdown filename="Prompt to paste into Claude Code (captured run)"}
Add a column country with the country of the organization. Change nothing
else. Run it again and show me the number of rows per country.
```

```r
# Country of the organization. The page does not list it, so it is inferred
# from the organization name: the first matching pattern below wins, and
# anything unmatched is treated as United States (the large majority).
# ... "DTUM" is read as TUM (Munich).
country_patterns <- c(
  "Australia"    = "Monash|New South Wales|University of Sydney",
  "Canada"       = "Alberta|Calgary|Ottawa",
  ...                                        # sixteen entries in all
)
placements$country <- "United States"
```

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

- It listed the 107 organizations, then typed sixteen patterns and a
  default. 77 rows are "United States" because no pattern matched.
- Its reply: the page does not list countries, so they are inferred;
  the non-US assignments "all look right".

::: {.notes}
Read the green lines in the box. Every country name in them is a fact
the page does not contain.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

The same shape of prompt as the postdoc flag, and a different kind of
answer. The tool listed the 107 distinct organizations, looked up five
of them it did not recognize, and then typed into the script a table of
sixteen patterns mapping fragments of organization names to countries,
with a default: every organization no pattern matches is "United
States". It ran the script and reported the counts, 77 United States,
7 China, 4 India, and so on, and added that the page does not list
countries, that they are therefore inferred from the names, and that
the non-US assignments "all look right". Two judgment calls were
flagged: "DTUM", which it read as the Technical University of Munich,
and international organizations counted at their headquarters.

The block as written, in full:

```{.r filename="code/placements.R (the country block, prompt 3)"}
# Country of the organization. The page does not list it, so it is inferred
# from the organization name: the first matching pattern below wins, and
# anything unmatched is treated as United States (the large majority).
# International organizations (IMF, World Bank, IDB, USAID) are assigned the
# country of their headquarters. "DTUM" is read as TUM (Munich).
country_patterns <- c(
  "Australia"    = "Monash|New South Wales|University of Sydney",
  "Canada"       = "Alberta|Calgary|Ottawa",
  "China"        = "Beijing|Peking|Renmin|Industrial and Commercial Bank of China|Xi.an Jiaotong",
  "Finland"      = "Finland",
  "France"       = "Paris School of Economics",
  "Germany"      = "Ludwig-Maximilian|DTUM",
  "Hong Kong"    = "Hong Kong",
  "India"        = "Azim Premji|Indian Institute of Management|IIMA|Krea",
  "New Zealand"  = "New Zealand",
  "Norway"       = "Norwegian",
  "Saudi Arabia" = "KAPSARC",
  "Singapore"    = "Nanyang|^NUS$",
  "South Korea"  = "KDI",
  "Switzerland"  = "Bern",
  "Vietnam"      = "VNUHCM",
  "Zambia"       = "Zambia"
)
placements$country <- "United States"
for (ctry in names(country_patterns)) {
  hit <- grepl(country_patterns[[ctry]], placements$organization) &
    placements$country == "United States"
  placements$country[hit] <- ctry
}
```

:::

## Where the countries came from {#countries-lesson}

- The page names a place for 14 of 109 rows. Nothing else on the page
  says a country.
- The rest is memory: a table it typed, and a default. It said so, in
  a comment and in its reply, and the column still went into the CSV.
- DTUM: Denmark in one run, Germany in the next. Same prompt, same page.
- Plausible is not the same as right. A fact it did not read is a
  guess, however confident the sentence around it.
- The script ran without error both times.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
Two runs on the same evening. Ask the room which one is right. Nobody
in the room knows, and that is the answer: it is not data.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

Count what the page supports. Fourteen of the 109 organization strings
name a place ("University of Alberta, Canada", "KDI School ... (Korea)",
"Federal Home Loan Bank of Topeka, KS"). For the other 95 the page says
nothing, and the tool cannot read a country from a name; it can only
remember one. The table it typed is a set of claims about the world,
and the default is a larger one: 77 rows became "United States" because
no pattern matched them, which is the same fate for "Clarkson
University" and for an organization it had never heard of.

The tool was honest about it. The comment says "inferred", the reply
says the page has no country field, and it flagged the two entries it
was least sure of. Honesty in the transcript does not change what is in
the CSV: a country column with no source, ready to be mapped, tabulated
and cited.

Run the same prompt twice and the guess moves. On the same evening, the
first run read "DTUM" as DTU Management in Denmark; the second, from
the same page with the same prompt, read it as the Technical University
of Munich in Germany. Both runs wrote a country, both ran without error,
and both replies said the assignments looked right. That is what
"plausible is not the same as right" looks like in a column.

:::

## What would have caught it earlier {#catch-earlier}

1. **A plan before code.** "Describe your approach before writing any
   code." The captured reply proposes a lookup table it would "populate
   myself from knowledge of the institutions" and mark "the handful I'm
   unsure about". You read that and say no.
2. **Question 4 of the five.** Names and constants yours? A
   sixteen-entry table of literals is a constant you did not supply.
3. **A reviewer with fresh eyes.** A second Claude that never saw this
   conversation, later today, found it in one turn.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
All three are cheap. The plan costs one sentence in the prompt and one
minute of reading.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

Three habits from the first part of this page would each have caught
the column before it existed. The cheapest is the plan. Sent on the
same project before prompt 3, "Describe your approach before writing
any code" produced the reply below: a hand-curated lookup table, filled
in "from knowledge of the institutions", with the uncertain ones
flagged. A reader who owns the question stops there: the source is the
model's memory, so the column is not wanted in that form.

The second is question 4 of the five questions for any diff: are the
names and constants yours? A table of sixteen literals is a constant,
and you did not supply it. The third is a reviewer that never saw the
conversation, the subagent in the seventh part of this page, which
reported the table and the default with line numbers in one turn.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## The captured plan reply, in full

````{.default}
⏺ Reply:
  Here's what I found and what I'd do.
  
  **What's there.** `code/placements.R` scrapes the Dyson placements table and writes `data/placements.csv` (109 rows; columns `year, name, position, organization, postdoc`). The `organization` column has ~105 distinct free-text strings — mixed granularity (`"Brown"`, `"NUS"`, `"DTUM"`, `"Stout"`), embedded departments (`"Purdue University, Department of Agricultural Economics"`), occasional location hints (`"Peking University (Beijing)"`, `"KDI School … (Korea)"`, `"University of Alberta, Canada"`), and a few two-organization entries (`"National Bureau of Economic Research, Claremont McKenna College"`).
  
  **Approach: a hand-curated lookup table, joined in the script.**
  
  1. **New file `data/org_country.csv`** with two columns, `organization, country`, one row per distinct organization string exactly as it appears in the scraped data (after `trimws`). I'd populate it myself from knowledge of the institutions, and mark the handful I'm unsure about in my reply so you can check them.
  2. **Edit `code/placements.R`**: after the `postdoc` flag and before `write.csv`, read the lookup, `match()` on the exact organization string, and add `placements$country`. If any organization isn't in the table, print the unmapped names and leave `country = NA` (warn rather than stop, so a re-scrape never fails when a new graduate appears — you just extend the table). Column order: `year, name, position, organization, country, postdoc`.
  
  **Why a lookup table rather than the alternatives.**
  - Regex heuristics ("University of X" → US) break immediately on `University of Sydney`, `University of Bern`, `University of Calgary`.
  - Geocoding / ROR / web APIs add a network dependency and choke on abbreviations like `NUS`, `IIMA`, `DTUM`, `Brown`.
  - The dataset is ~100 rows; a table is trivial to maintain, fully reproducible, and the script rewrites `placements.csv` on every run, so the mapping has to live outside that file anyway.
  
  **Judgment calls I'd make unless you say otherwise.**
  - **Country labels:** plain English short names (`United States`, `United Kingdom`, `South Korea`, `Hong Kong`, …). I can add an ISO3 code column too if you want it for later joins.
  - **International organizations** (World Bank, IMF, Inter-American Development Bank, USAID): `United States` — headquarters location. Alternative is a separate "International" label; say which you prefer.
  - **Hong Kong**: `Hong Kong`, not `China`.
  - **Multinationals** (Uber, Citibank, Morgan Stanley, Capital One, StoneX, Acadian): country of headquarters (US), since the `position` text doesn't give an office location.
  - **Two-org entries**: country of the first-listed organization (both examples are US anyway).
  - **Uncertain ones I'd flag:** `DTUM` (likely DTU Management, Denmark), `Stout` (US consulting firm), `Cooper/Smith` (US), `Econic Partners LLC` (US), `Center for Governmental Research` (US, Rochester NY).
  
  If that all sounds right — or you want ISO codes / a different rule for international orgs — tell me and I'll write it.
````

:::

## The fix: facts you supply live in a data file {#fix-countries}

```{.markdown filename="Prompt to paste into Claude Code (captured run)"}
The page does not state countries, so the lookup is a guess. Replace it: write
the distinct organizations to data/countries.csv with an empty country column
for me to fill in, read that file in the script, and set country to NA when
the organization is not in it or its country is empty. Change nothing else.
Run it and tell me how many rows have NA.
```

```r
countries <- read.csv(file.path("data", "countries.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
countries$country[trimws(countries$country) == ""] <- NA
placements$country <- countries$country[match(placements$organization,
                                              countries$organization)]
```

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

- `data/countries.csv`: 107 organizations, an empty country column,
  written once.
- 109 of 109 rows are `NA` until you fill it. The CSV claims nothing
  nobody checked.
- Fill ten rows from the organizations' pages, run, commit the file.

::: {.notes}
The tool did the plumbing: the file, the match, the NA. The facts are
yours to type, and git records that you typed them.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

The fix keeps the plumbing and moves the facts. The prompt says what is
wrong (the lookup is a guess), what to do instead (a data file with the
organizations, filled in by you), and what to do with the gaps (`NA`).
The tool wrote `data/countries.csv` once, 107 rows with an empty
`country` column, replaced the pattern table with three lines that read
the file and match on the organization, ran the script, and reported
that all 109 rows have `NA`. That is the right answer for now: the
column claims nothing until a person supplies a fact.

Filling the file is research, not typing: each country comes from the
organization's own page, and a row you cannot settle stays empty. Commit
the file with a message that says the countries are yours. From then on
the fact, its source and who supplied it are in the record, and the
script never invents a country for a new organization; it prints `NA`
and waits for you.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}

````{.default}
  -     placements$country == "United States"
  -   placements$country[hit] <- ctry
  - }
  + # Country of the organization. The page does not list it, so it is looked up
  + # in data/countries.csv (organization, country), a hand-filled file. Any
  + # organization missing from that file, or with an empty country, gets NA.
  + countries <- read.csv(file.path("data", "countries.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  + countries$country[trimws(countries$country) == ""] <- NA
  + placements$country <- countries$country[match(placements$organization,
  +                                               countries$organization)]
  ⎿ The file <project>code/placements.R has been updated successfully.
⏺ Bash(Rscript code/placements.R && Rscript -e 'p <- read.csv("data/placements.csv"); cat("NA country:", sum(is.na(p$country)), "of", nrow(p), "\n")')
  ⎿ Wrote 109 rows to data/placements.csv 
    NA country: 109 of 109
⏺ Reply:
  Done.
  
  - `data/countries.csv` — 107 distinct organizations (sorted), `country` column empty for you to fill in. Written once as a one-off; the script only reads it, so it won't overwrite your entries.
  - `code/placements.R:39-45` — the hardcoded pattern table and `"United States"` default are gone. The script now reads `data/countries.csv`, treats empty countries as NA, and assigns `country` via `match()` on the organization; unmatched organizations get NA. Nothing else changed.
  
  Ran it: **109 of 109 rows have NA** for `country`, as expected since the file is still blank.
````

:::

## Exercise 2 {#exercise-2 .smaller}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Exercise

```bash
# Exercise 2 (8 minutes). Same project: Claude Code in Terminal 1, git in
# Terminal 2.
#
# 1. On the page, Ctrl+F (Cmd+F on a Mac): "postdoc", "post-doc",
#    "post doc". Add the three counts. Write the sum down.

# 2. Paste Prompt 2 (postdoc). Read the edit box: which spellings does

#
# 3. Paste Prompt 3 (country). Read the edit box before 1. Yes: where
#    does each country come from? Count the country names typed into
#    the code. Then 1. Yes, and read the table it prints.
#
# 4. Terminal 2: git diff. How many + lines are facts the page does not
#    contain?
#
# 5. Paste the fix prompt (previous section). Read the box, 1. Yes.
#    Terminal 2: git status, then git add -A and a commit whose message
#    says which lines are the tool's.

```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

*Paired up?* Swap roles: the reader from Exercise 1 types now. In step
3, the reader says each country aloud and the typist says whether the
page states it. In step 5, the box shows red lines for the whole
pattern table; that is the removal you asked for.

### Solution

Step 1: 15 + 9 + 1 = 25 when captured. Step 2: the box names three or
four spellings; the count matches. Step 3: about sixteen country names
in the code, plus "United States" as the default, none from the page.
Step 4: every `+` line with a country name in it. Step 5: `git status`
lists `code/placements.R` modified and `data/countries.csv` new; after
the commit, `git log --oneline` starts with your message.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

**25**; sixteen names plus a default, none from the page; DTUM varies
from run to run (Denmark and Germany on the same evening); after the
fix, 109 `NA`.

::: {.notes}
Debrief (2 min). Hands: who got Denmark for DTUM, who got Germany, who
got something else? Same prompt, same page. Then: who read the box and
pressed Esc instead of 1. Yes? That was the right call too; the fix
prompt works from either state.

When it fails, say:

- The pattern matched fewer than the page count: it matched one
  spelling; the check would have caught it; ask for a patch naming the
  missing spelling.
- No country table, it wrote NA for everything: a better run than the
  captured one; read its reply for why, and go to step 5 anyway.
- It asked to fetch the organizations' web pages: Esc; that is a
  different task, and today the facts are yours to supply.
- `git diff` shows the postdoc line removed: "Change nothing else" was
  not held; `git restore code/placements.R` and ask again.

## CLAUDE.md: standing instructions, read at every launch {#claude-md}

- A markdown file at the root, read at every launch.
- Layout, style, facts and checks, working rules. Nothing that changes
  per task.
- Short: 35 lines here. The docs' target is under 200.
- Committed. It is part of the record.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
Everything you would otherwise paste into every prompt, written once.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

[`CLAUDE.md`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory) is a markdown file
at the repository root that Claude Code reads at the start of every
session in that folder. It holds what every prompt would otherwise
repeat: the layout, the coding conventions, the working rules. Keep it
short; the one here is 35 lines, and the docs' target is under 200. You
commit it with the repository, so it shows in `git diff` and travels
with the code.

:::

Type `/init` at the prompt. It reads the folder and proposes a
`CLAUDE.md`, shown in the same approval box as any new file. Accept it,
read it, and treat it as a draft: it describes what it found, not what
you want, and it knows nothing about where facts may come from. The
next section replaces it.

```{.markdown filename="CLAUDE.md"}
# placements

Conventions for any code written in this repository.

## Layout

- `code/` holds one script per task. `data/` holds what scripts read and
  write; `data/countries.csv` is filled in by hand and never overwritten.
- Scripts run from the project root, from a clean R session, with
  relative paths like `"data/placements.csv"`.

## Style

- Base R. The only package is `rvest`, and only for reading HTML.
- Short lower-case names with underscores: `by_year`, `n_postdoc`.
- A number or a URL that could change sits at the top of the script as a
  named constant in capitals: `URL <- "..."`.
- Every script starts with a comment saying what it reads and what it
  writes.
- Comments say why, not what.
- A function does one job and returns a value; the script calls it.

## Facts and checks

- A fact that is not on the page and not in a data file does not go into
  code. Put it in a file under `data/` that I fill in, and use `NA` until
  I do.
- After a merge or a filter, check the row count with `stopifnot()`.

## Working rules

- Do not run scripts unless the prompt asks. I run them in RStudio.
- Do not create files I did not ask for. Do not edit `.gitignore` or the
  `.Rproj` file.
- Do not use git unless the prompt asks. I commit.
```

:::

## Style habits in CLAUDE.md: naming, structure, constants, comments {#style-in-claude-md}

- **Naming**: `snake_case`; file names say what the script does.
- **Structure**: one script per task; a function does one job.
- **Named constants**: `URL <- "..."` at the top, never a bare value
  below.
- **Comments say why**, not what. A header on every script.
- **Facts and checks**: a fact not on the page goes in a data file; a
  row count after every merge.
- Written once. Read at every launch. Copy it to the next repository.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
Your style sheet is how you brief an assistant. It is also how you brief
yourself in December. The five habits are the style handout; this is
where it pays off.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

The Style section is the personal part. Names in `snake_case`, file
names that say what the script does. One script per task; a function
does one job and the script calls it. Numbers that could change sit at
the top as named constants in capitals. Comments say why, not what.
These are the habits you use when you write code yourself; written
down, they are the brief an assistant reads at every launch. The "Facts
and checks" section is the one this project taught: a fact the tool did
not read goes into a data file you fill, and a row count follows every
merge. Copy the Style and the Facts sections from one repository to the
next; the Layout section is the one that changes.

:::

## A one-sentence prompt after CLAUDE.md {#short-prompt}

```{.markdown filename="Prompt to paste into Claude Code (captured run)"}
Write code/by_year.R: for each year, the number of placements and the number
of postdocs, from data/placements.csv, printed as a table with one row per
year.
```

```r
# Reads data/placements.csv. Writes nothing; prints a table with one row
# per year giving the number of placements and the number of postdocs.

PLACEMENTS <- "data/placements.csv"

count_by_year <- function(placements) {
  ...
  # Every placement belongs to exactly one year, so the counts must add up.
  stopifnot(sum(by_year$n_placements) == nrow(placements))
  by_year
}
```

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

- Not in the prompt: the header, the constant, the function, the row
  check, "do not run it". All in `CLAUDE.md`.
- Its last sentence: "Not run, per the project rules."

::: {.notes}
What is missing from the prompt is in the file it read at launch. The
check on the counts came from the "Facts and checks" section.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

With `CLAUDE.md` in place, one sentence asked for a small script. What
came back has a header saying what it reads and writes, the path as a
named constant, a function that does one job and returns a value, a
`stopifnot()` that the per-year counts add up to the row count, and a
reply ending "Not run, per the project rules." None of that was in the
prompt; all of it was in the file. The full script:

```{.r filename="code/by_year.R"}
# Reads data/placements.csv. Writes nothing; prints a table with one row
# per year giving the number of placements and the number of postdocs.

PLACEMENTS <- "data/placements.csv"

count_by_year <- function(placements) {
  n_placements <- tapply(placements$postdoc, placements$year, length)
  n_postdoc <- tapply(placements$postdoc, placements$year, sum)
  by_year <- data.frame(
    year = as.integer(names(n_placements)),
    n_placements = as.integer(n_placements),
    n_postdoc = as.integer(n_postdoc)
  )
  # Every placement belongs to exactly one year, so the counts must add up.
  stopifnot(sum(by_year$n_placements) == nrow(placements))
  by_year
}

placements <- read.csv(PLACEMENTS)
by_year <- count_by_year(placements)
print(by_year, row.names = FALSE)
```

Sourced in RStudio, it prints one row per year, 2015 to 2026, with the
number of placements and of postdocs. Conventions go in the file; the
task, and any fact the tool might otherwise guess, still go in the
prompt.

:::

## Subagents: a second Claude with its own context {#subagents}

- A subagent is a separate conversation the tool starts for one task:
  its own empty context, its own tool list, `CLAUDE.md` included. It
  returns a report, not its working.
- When: reading many files, so your context stays small; an
  independent review of a diff or a rule, so the checker is not the
  thing being checked.
- One line: `Use a subagent to review code/x.R against this rule: ...
  Report what it says. Do not edit anything.`
- Permanent: a file in `.claude/agents/`, like `CLAUDE.md`: a name, a
  description, the tools it may use, then its instructions.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
The reviewer never saw the conversation that wrote the code. That is
the point, and it is the same rule as typing the check yourself.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

A [subagent](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents) is a second
conversation that the tool starts for one task and closes when the task
is done. It begins with an empty context: the task, `CLAUDE.md`, and
nothing from your conversation, not the files already read, not the
prompt that wrote the code. It has its own list of tools, which can be
shorter than the main conversation's. When it finishes, its report
comes back into your conversation as text; its reading and its
intermediate steps stay in its own context and are gone.

Two uses fit this course. The first is reading: a task that opens many
files fills your context with their contents, and everything the model
has in front of it competes for its attention; a subagent reads them in
its own context and reports a summary. The second is review: a reviewer
that did not see the conversation that produced the code judges the
code on its own terms. That is the rule from the check section, the
checker is not the thing being checked, applied inside the tool. The
docs recommend the same step before treating a task as done, a review
of the diff in a fresh context, and warn that a reviewer asked to find
gaps will report some even when the work is sound; ask for gaps that
affect correctness, not style.

Two ways to use one. The one-line way needs no setup: "Use a subagent
to review code/x.R against this rule: ... Report what it says. Do not
edit anything." The tool starts a general-purpose subagent with that
task. The permanent way is a file in `.claude/agents/` at the
repository root, committed like `CLAUDE.md`: a name, a description of
when it applies, the tools it may use, then its instructions in plain
prose. The `tools:` line is a fence. A reviewer allowed only `Read`,
`Grep` and `Glob` cannot edit a file whatever its instructions say. You
call it by name in a prompt. The next section shows one.

A subagent is one more model call, with its own cost, and its report is
a claim like any transcript: the line it quotes is what you check.

:::

## A read-only reviewer subagent: the file {#reviewer-agent}

```{.markdown filename=".claude/agents/hand-check-reviewer.md"}
---
name: hand-check-reviewer
description: Reviews one R script against one rule from the request. Read-only.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob
---

You review one R script against one rule given in the request. Read the
script. Reply in three lines: the rule; the line of code that follows it
or breaks it, quoted; the verdict, "follows" or "breaks". Do not edit any
file. Do not propose a rewrite unless asked.
```

- Save, commit, relaunch. The name is how you call it.
- `tools:` is the fence: it can read; it cannot edit or run anything.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
Same shape as CLAUDE.md: written once, read when called. The body is
its standing instructions; the request supplies the rule.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

The file, as used in the captured run. In RStudio: File → New File →
Text File, paste, save as `.claude/agents/hand-check-reviewer.md`
(RStudio's Files pane hides folders that start with a dot; Show Hidden
Files in the pane's More menu, or type the path in the save dialog).
Commit it: `git add .claude/agents/hand-check-reviewer.md`, then a
commit message. Relaunch Claude Code so it reads the folder. The
frontmatter between the `---` lines names the agent, says when it
applies, and lists its tools; the prose below is its standing
instructions, the way `CLAUDE.md` holds the repository's. The rule to
check against comes with each request.

:::


```{.default filename="The subagent's report, condensed; the full report is on the page"}
No data file is read anywhere; the only input is read_html(url) on line 10.
```

::: {.notes}
Same rule as typing the check yourself: the checker is not the thing

:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

Sent on the project after prompt 3, before the fix. The main
conversation started the subagent with the rule and the file name; the
subagent read the script and returned the report; the main conversation
relayed it, with the line numbers, and added that nothing was edited.
